style_1_icd10.name: Photocontact dermatitis [berloque dermatitis]
style_1_icd10.chapter: XII. Diseases of the skin and subcutaneous tissue / Dermatology (L00-L99)

style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: AAD Guidelines of Care for the Management of Atopic Dermatitis (2024) / EADV Guidelines

clinical_targets.goal: ≥ 75% reduction in Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-75) from baseline
Pruritus NRS score ≤ 3 (or ≥ 4-point reduction from baseline)
Restoration of epidermal barrier and complete resolution of eczema-induced sleep disturbance

steps_summary: Step 1: Baseline Maintenance & Mild Acute Flaring

steps.title: Baseline Maintenance & Mild Acute Flaring
steps.rationale: Aggressive skin barrier hydration with ceramide/lipid-rich emollients applied immediately post-bathing. When flaring, initiate low-to-mid potency topical corticosteroids or non-steroidal topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs).

drug_classes.role: First-line suppression of cutaneous T-cell inflammation and pruritus during mild flares.
drug_classes.dosing: Hydrocortisone 1%–2.5% cream (Class VII) for face/folds; Mometasone furoate 0.1% cream (Class IV) once daily for trunk/limbs.
drug_classes.pearls: Use lowest effective potency for 1–2 weeks until clear, then step down or switch to intermittent proactive maintenance (twice weekly).

drug_classes.role: Steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory agents with zero risk of cutaneous atrophy.
drug_classes.dosing: Pimecrolimus 1% cream for mild-moderate eczema on sensitive areas; Tacrolimus 0.03%–0.1% ointment for moderate-to-severe lesions.
drug_classes.pearls: Preferred on delicate skin (eyelids, face, neck, groin/intertriginous zones) to prevent steroid-induced skin thinning. Counsel patients that transient burning/stinging usually subsides within 3–5 days.

steps.title: Moderate-to-Severe Eczema Flare
steps.rationale: Intensify anti-inflammatory therapy with potent topical corticosteroids to rapidly gain control, combined with sedative antihistamines if nocturnal pruritus disrupts sleep.

drug_classes.role: Rapid containment of marked erythema, edema, and excoriations on thick lichenified skin.
drug_classes.dosing: Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% or Mometasone 0.1% ointment applied in a thin film once or twice daily for up to 2–3 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Ointment vehicles are superior to creams for dry, lichenified lesions because they provide occlusion and do not contain stinging alcohol preservatives.

steps.title: Severe Recalcitrant Atopic Dermatitis
steps.rationale: When disease is refractory to optimized topical therapies and wet-wrap therapy, escalate to super-potent short pulses on stubborn lichenified plaques or systemic non-biologic immunosuppression.

drug_classes.role: Short-pulse therapy for dense chronic lichenified flexural plaques.
drug_classes.dosing: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment applied sparingly once daily for max 2 consecutive weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Never use on the face, groin, or axillae. Do not exceed 50 g/week to prevent hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression.

drug_classes.role: Systemic disease control in extensive, disabling, therapy-resistant disease.
drug_classes.dosing: Methotrexate 10–25 mg orally once weekly with mandatory Folic Acid 5 mg weekly.
drug_classes.pearls: Slow onset (takes 8–12 weeks for maximal benefit). Requires strict monitoring of CBC, LFTs, and renal function.

pearls: Use lowest effective potency for 1–2 weeks until clear, then step down or switch to intermittent proactive maintenance (twice weekly).

Preferred on delicate skin (eyelids, face, neck, groin/intertriginous zones) to prevent steroid-induced skin thinning. Counsel patients that transient burning/stinging usually subsides within 3–5 days.
Ointment vehicles are superior to creams for dry, lichenified lesions because they provide occlusion and do not contain stinging alcohol preservatives.
Never use on the face, groin, or axillae. Do not exceed 50 g/week to prevent hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression.

special_populations.pediatric: Children have high body surface area-to-mass ratio; use low-potency steroids (Hydrocortisone 1%) or TCIs on delicate areas. Avoid potent steroids under occlusion or in diaper area.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Emollients are first-line. Mild-to-moderate topical corticosteroids (Hydrocortisone, Mometasone) are preferred when pharmacotherapy is needed.

style_3_monograph.summary: A rash is an area of irritated or swollen skin. Many rashes are itchy, red, painful, and irritated. Some rashes can also lead to blisters or patches of raw skin. Rashes are a symptom of many different medical problems. Other causes include irritating substances and allergies. Certain genes can make people more likely to get rashes. Contact dermatitis is a common type of rash. It causes redness, itching, and sometimes small bumps. You get the rash where you have touched an irritant, such as a chemical, or something you are allergic to, like poison ivy . Some rashes develop right away. Others form over several days. Although most rashes clear up fairly quickly, others are long-lasting and need long-term treatment. Because rashes can be caused by many different things, it's important to figure out what kind you have before you treat it. If it is a bad rash, if it does not go away, or if you have other symptoms, you should see your health care provider. Treatments may include moisturizers, lotions, baths, cortisone creams that relieve swelling, and antihistamines, which relieve itching.
style_3_monograph.treatment: Your provider will recommend treatment based on what is causing the problem. In some cases, the best treatment is to do nothing to the area. Often, treatment includes washing the area with a lot of water to get rid of any traces of the irritant that are still on the skin. You should avoid further exposure to the substance. Emollients or moisturizers help keep the skin moist, and also help skin repair itself. They protect the skin from becoming inflamed again. They are a key part of preventing and treating irritant contact dermatitis. Topical corticosteroid medicines are commonly used to treat contact dermatitis. Topical means you place it on the skin. You will be prescribed a cream or ointment. Topical corticosteroids may also be called topical steroids or topical cortisones. Do not use more medicine or use it more often than your provider advises you to use it. Your provider may also prescribe other creams or ointments, such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, to use on the skin. In severe cases, you may need to take corticosteroid pills. Your provider will start you on a high dose and your dose will be slowly reduced over about 12 days. You may also receive a corticosteroid shot. Wet dressings and soothing anti-itch (antipruritic) lotions may be recommended to reduce other symptoms. Topical corticosteroids should be used only for short periods. Long-term use increases the risk of developing more irritant contact dermatitis.
